lessons.title: Why Almost Every Real Quantum Application Is Hybrid

slots.practicalActivity: Write a short explanation (3-4 sentences) of why a proposed architecture where 'the quantum part decides when the job is done, handing control back to classical code only at the end' cannot be built on current quantum cloud hardware, citing specifically what a QPU can and cannot do per this lesson. Then redraw the lesson's classical-control-loop architecture diagram for a use case of your own choosing, labeling which box does which job.
slots.deliverable: Your written explanation of why the proposed architecture is impossible today, plus your own redrawn architecture diagram labeled for a self-chosen use case.

slots.practicalActivity: A variational circuit has 12 parameters. Using the parameter-shift rule's formula (2 x params + 1), compute how many circuit evaluations one iteration requires. Then compute the total cost of running 100 iterations at 500 shots each on a backend charging $0.30/task + $0.01/shot, and propose one concrete change that would reduce that cost without changing the final accuracy requirement.
slots.deliverable: Your evaluations-per-iteration calculation, the total 100-iteration cost, and a written cost-reduction proposal.

lessons.title: Quantum as a Coprocessor vs. Quantum as the Whole Program

slots.practicalActivity: A manager asks you to scope a project that factors 2048-bit RSA keys using Shor's algorithm 'as the whole quantum program, no classical loop needed, since it's a textbook algorithm.' Using this lesson's Pattern A vs. Pattern B distinction and its comparison table, write what's wrong with scoping this as a near-term buildable project and what you'd actually tell the manager.
slots.deliverable: Your written response to the manager, naming which pattern the request assumes and explaining why it is not buildable on current hardware.

slots.practicalActivity: Apply this lab's four-question method (loop or one-shot? what's the QPU's job? how many evaluations? does the scale exist today?) to a new ticket: 'Use quantum computing to speed up our nightly SQL batch ETL job.' Walk through all four questions explicitly, the same way the lab worked through its three tickets, and reach a verdict.
slots.deliverable: Your written four-question walkthrough and final verdict on the SQL-ETL ticket, in the same format as the lab's three worked tickets.

slots.practicalActivity: Your team's VQE loop has been running for three hours with no convergence and no cost alert. Using Mistakes 1, 3, and 4 from this lesson, write a short post-incident note explaining which of these mistakes most likely contributed, and the specific classical-code fix for each one you identify.
slots.deliverable: Your written post-incident note naming the contributing mistakes (1, 3, and/or 4) and their specific fixes.

slots.practicalActivity: You have a classical feature vector [2,2,2,2]. Compute its normalized form for amplitude encoding by hand (show the sum of squares, the norm, and the resulting normalized vector), state how many qubits it needs, and verify the normalized vector's squared entries sum to 1. Then repeat the entire process on your own for the vector [1,3,5,7].
slots.deliverable: Your worked normalization for [2,2,2,2] and a second worked normalization for your own [1,3,5,7] vector, each with the required qubit count stated.

slots.practicalActivity: A 30-parameter circuit is optimized with 80 iterations of parameter-shift versus an estimated 240 iterations of SPSA (3x more, accounting for its noisier gradient estimate) to reach comparable accuracy. At 500 shots/eval on a backend charging $0.30/task + $0.01/shot, compute the total cost for each approach.
slots.deliverable: Your two total-cost calculations (parameter-shift vs. SPSA) and a written recommendation stating which you'd choose and why.

slots.practicalActivity: Two circuit submissions for the same observable returned: submission A, 800 shots, counts {0:500, 1:300}; submission B, 200 shots (a partial retry), counts {0:140, 1:60}. Compute the correctly shot-weighted combined expectation value, and separately compute what a naive unweighted average of the two circuits' individual expectation values would give.
slots.deliverable: Your two computed expectation values (shot-weighted and naive-averaged) plus a written explanation of why they differ.

slots.practicalActivity: Write out, in pseudocode or prose, a known-answer unit test for the shot-weighted aggregation logic from Lesson 8, using two synthetic circuit submissions whose correct combined expectation value you compute by hand before writing the test.
slots.deliverable: Your two stated synthetic inputs, your hand-computed expected output, and the unit test itself (pseudocode or prose).

slots.practicalActivity: Your orchestration code needs to estimate the cost of the same 500-shot circuit on both an AWS Braket IonQ device and an IBM Quantum Pay-As-You-Go device. Explain why a single cost = shots x price_per_shot formula works for one provider but not the other, and write out what information your estimate_cost() adapter would need for each provider specifically.
slots.deliverable: Your written explanation of the pricing-dimension mismatch, plus the two providers' distinct estimate_cost() input requirements.

lessons.title: Orchestrating a Pipeline Across Classical & Quantum Compute

slots.practicalActivity: Using the unbatched/batched timing model from this lesson, compute the total wall-clock time for a 60-iteration run (instead of 150) under both the unbatched and batched approaches, and state the speedup factor. Then describe, in terms of the orchestration layer's responsibilities, what would actually have to change in the code (not just the math) to realize the batched version's speedup in production.
slots.deliverable: Your two 60-iteration total-time calculations, the resulting speedup factor, and a written description of the required orchestration code change.

lessons.title: Error Handling for Remote Quantum Jobs

slots.practicalActivity: A job fails with a circuit validation error on its first attempt. Your orchestration code's generic retry handler resubmits it automatically three times before giving up. Using this lesson's retryable-vs-fallback decision table, explain what's wrong with this behavior and write the correct handling logic instead.
slots.deliverable: Your written explanation of why retrying a validation failure is wrong, plus the corrected handling logic you would implement instead.

lessons.title: Retry & Fallback Strategies for Queued Hardware

slots.practicalActivity: Using a base delay of 1,000ms and a cap of 30,000ms, compute the deterministic exponential backoff delay for attempts 0 through 4, and the total worst-case wait across those 5 attempts. Then, using this lesson's three fallback options, choose and justify which one you'd use for a time-sensitive production job that has exhausted all 5 retries.
slots.deliverable: Your 5-attempt backoff delay calculation with the total worst-case wait, plus your chosen fallback option with written justification.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the per-iteration cost of $20.40 and a 150-iteration run, compute the total cost if 20 iterations (instead of this lab's 10) each require exactly one failed billed attempt before succeeding. Calculate what percentage of total spend the wasted-retry cost represents, and write a judgment on whether this device is a good choice for this workload going forward.
slots.deliverable: Your total-cost calculation at 20 failed iterations, the wasted-spend percentage, and your written judgment on the device's suitability for this workload.

slots.practicalActivity: A job needs 50 tasks at 2,000 shots each. Compute its total cost on IonQ Harmony ($0.30/task + $0.01/shot) both with and without program-set batching, and state the dollar and percentage savings from batching.
slots.deliverable: Your two total-cost calculations (with and without batching) and the resulting dollar and percentage savings.

slots.practicalActivity: A device's observed average queue wait rises from 38 seconds to 90 seconds during a high-demand period. Recompute the batched per-iteration total and the full 150-iteration batched total under this new queue wait, and write what you'd tell a stakeholder who asks why the estimate changed.
slots.deliverable: Your recomputed per-iteration and 150-iteration totals at the higher queue wait, plus your written stakeholder explanation.

slots.practicalActivity: A use case needs a standard error of 0.015 or better. Using the 1/sqrt(shots) relationship and the fact that 1,000 shots gives a standard error of 0.0316, compute the minimum number of shots needed to meet this target, then compute the total cost for a 100-task job at that shot count on IonQ Harmony ($0.30/task + $0.01/shot).
slots.deliverable: Your minimum-shots calculation for a 0.015 standard error, plus the resulting total cost for the 100-task job.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the production workload from this lab (150 iterations, 17 evals/iteration, originally 2,000 shots/eval, daily, 22 days/month), recompute the monthly cost if shots are reduced to 500/eval AND the job runs weekly (4.4 times/month) instead of daily. Determine whether this combination fits the $3,000/month prod budget.
slots.deliverable: Your recomputed monthly cost under the combined shots-and-frequency change, and a stated verdict on whether it fits the $3,000 budget.

lessons.title: Project Kickoff: Define the Hybrid Workflow

slots.practicalActivity: Using the four-question method, write a one-paragraph scoping judgment for this alternative ticket: 'Run this same molecular ground-state estimation hourly, every hour, 24/7, instead of once daily.' Use the lesson's $960/run figure to compute the resulting monthly cost, and write your recommendation on whether to approve it.
slots.deliverable: Your computed monthly cost for hourly/24-7 operation and your written scoping recommendation.

slots.practicalActivity: The orchestration layer's test harness forces iteration 23 (of 80) to return a FAILED status when run against the simulator. Walk through, step by step, what the state machine should do in response, citing the specific retry/fallback decision logic that applies, and explain how you'd confirm the test passed.
slots.deliverable: Your written step-by-step walkthrough of the state machine's response to the forced failure, plus your stated test-pass confirmation criteria.

lessons.title: Project: Add Error Handling & Cost Tracking

slots.practicalActivity: The cost circuit-breaker is set to $1,200 with 25% headroom over the $960 planned budget. If 5 iterations each incur one wasted $12.00 failed attempt before succeeding, compute the cumulative cost and determine whether the run completes all 80 iterations before the circuit-breaker would trip.
slots.deliverable: Your cumulative-cost calculation across the 5 wasted attempts plus a stated conclusion on whether the circuit-breaker trips before iteration 80.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a short sign-off review (3-5 sentences) for this capstone project, explicitly referencing at least three of the five Lesson 5 checklist rows with the specific evidence from this project that satisfies each one, and naming the one open item (the $21,120/month daily-run cost projection from kickoff) that should not be allowed to quietly disappear.
slots.deliverable: Your written 3-5 sentence sign-off review, citing three specific checklist rows with evidence and explicitly naming the open item.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can design, build, and operate a production-grade hybrid quantum-classical system: choosing Pattern A vs. Pattern B correctly, building a variational loop with proper data pre-processing and result aggregation, orchestrating batched job submission with retries and fallbacks across cloud quantum providers, and tracking cost, latency, and shot budgets with a circuit-breaker — the same engineering discipline the course's own capstone VQE project demonstrates end to end.
